content.title: About
content.content: Dumpling, No Meat is a ready‑to‑eat product that replaces the traditional meat filling with a plant‑based mixture of soy protein, mushrooms, vegetables and spices. The dough is made from wheat flour, water and salt, and the finished product is flash‑frozen for long‑term storage.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Meat‑free dumplings are popular among vegetarians and those reducing animal protein intake.
The filling often contains soy protein and mushrooms, which give a "meaty" taste and texture.
The product can be stored in the freezer for up to 12 months without quality loss.
Traditional preparation is boiling in salted water for 5‑7 minutes after thawing.
In some markets they are sold under labels such as "vegan dumplings".

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Soy protein in the filling provides a complete amino‑acid profile useful for muscle maintenance and metabolism.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with conventional meat dumplings, this product contains less saturated fat, supporting cardiovascular health.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Vegetables and mushrooms add fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Soy protein and mushrooms supply B1, B2, B6 and folate, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Cholesterol‑free
items.content: Absence of animal ingredients makes the dumpling virtually cholesterol‑free.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to soy protein.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Salt is often added to dough and filling for flavor; people monitoring sodium intake should watch portion size.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: The wheat‑based dough contains gluten, making it unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

items.title: Proper cooking
items.content: Undercooked dumplings may harbor live microorganisms; always boil until fully cooked.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: After thawing, boil the dumplings in salted water for 5‑7 minutes until they float, then serve with sour cream, soy sauce or a vegetable sauce. They can also be pan‑fried after boiling for a crispy crust.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen dumplings in an airtight bag at –18 °C or lower. Once thawed, consume within 2‑3 days when stored in the refrigerator. Do not keep at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Pecan pie is a dessert featuring a flaky crust filled with a sweet mixture of ground pecans, sugar, butter, and eggs. The pecan (Carya illinoinensis) is a North American nut known for its buttery flavor and rich aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pecans belong to the hickory family and are more closely related to oak than to typical nuts.
In the United States, pecans are considered the national nut; Texas hosts an annual "Pecan Fest".
Pecan trees can live over 300 years and begin producing nuts after about 30 years.
The caramel sauce often used in the filling is traditionally made from molasses, a by‑product of sugarcane processing.
Pecans are high in antioxidants, especially flavonoids and phenolic acids.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Pecans provide vitamin E and polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Healthy monounsaturated fats
items.content: Most of the fat in pecans is monounsaturated, which supports heart health.

items.title: Source of magnesium
items.content: Magnesium aids normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The fiber in pecans promotes healthy digestion and satiety.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Pecans contain thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pecans, ranging from mild to anaphylaxis.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Pecan pie is calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: The filling often contains a lot of sugar, which can be problematic for people with diabetes.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Pecans contain oxalates that may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pecan pie is served as a dessert with tea or coffee. Slice into portions and enjoy warm or chilled. Leftover pieces store well in the refrigerator.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the pie in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze in freezer‑safe bags for up to 3 months. Allow it to come to room temperature before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: A graham cracker pie shell is a crisp, lightly sweet base made from whole‑grain flour, sugar, butter and spices. It is a staple in many American desserts, from cheesecakes to fruit tarts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Graham crackers were created in the early 19th century by Dr. Sylvester Graham as a healthier alternative to regular biscuits.
Traditional recipes use whole‑grain flour, honey and cinnamon, giving the cracker its distinctive aroma.
The shells are often used in no‑bake recipes – the crackers are crushed and mixed with melted butter.
Graham crackers are popular in the US, Canada and Australia, but less common in Europe.
Gluten‑free versions are made from rice or corn flour.

items.title: Source of whole grains
items.content: Whole‑grain flour provides dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many other cookies, graham crackers contain a moderate amount of fat, making them suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals aid energy metabolism and muscle function.

items.title: Antioxidant spices
items.content: Ingredients such as cinnamon have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional graham crackers contain wheat, so they are not suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: The crackers contain added sugar, which should be considered by those monitoring blood glucose.

items.title: Calorie density in large portions
items.content: Consuming large amounts can lead to excess calorie intake.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Crush the crackers into fine crumbs, combine with melted butter (usually 1:1 by weight), and press into a pan. After chilling, fill with cheesecake, fruit, custard, or any desired filling. The crumbs can also be used as a crunchy topping for ice cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the crackers in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent moisture absorption.

content.title: About
content.content: The sardine sandwich is a quick and nutritious snack made with whole‑grain bread, canned sardines, lettuce, a slice of tomato, and a light yogurt‑based sauce. Sardines are rich in omega‑3 fatty acids, protein, and B‑vitamins, making this sandwich a healthy option for lunch or a snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sardines are named after the island of Sardinia, where they have been traditionally fished in the Mediterranean Sea.
Canned sardines are often packed in oil or their own juice, preserving their nutritional value.
Sardines are one of the most sustainable fish species, with a low impact on marine ecosystems.
In Japan, sardines (sai) are frequently served as sushi, while in Portugal they are baked with potatoes.
The sardine sandwich is popular among athletes for its high protein and carbohydrate content.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Omega‑3 fatty acids support heart health and reduce inflammation.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: One sandwich provides about 20 g of protein, essential for muscle repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Sardines supply vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: When eaten with bones, sardines become a good source of calcium and vitamin D for bone strength.

items.title: Low mercury levels
items.content: Compared with large predatory fish, sardines contain minimal mercury, making them safe for frequent consumption.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including sardines.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned sardines can be high in salt; people with hypertension should choose low‑sodium versions.

items.title: Additive concerns
items.content: Certain cans may contain preservatives or flavor enhancers that are unsuitable for those sensitive to food additives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice whole‑grain bread, spread a light yogurt sauce, add lettuce, a tomato slice, and the sardines (with or without bones). Optionally include avocado slices or a dash of mustard. The sandwich can be eaten by hand or cut into bite‑size pieces for children.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The sandwich is best enjoyed fresh. If needed, wrap it tightly in plastic wrap and refrigerate for up to 24 hours. Canned sardines should be kept in a sealed jar in a cool, dry place until the printed expiration date.

tomato-and-vegetable-juice-100-low-sodiu.title: Tomato and Vegetable Juice 100%, Low Sodium

content.title: About
content.content: Tomato and vegetable juice 100% is a ready‑to‑drink beverage made from ripe tomatoes and a blend of vegetables (carrot, celery, pepper). The juice contains no added sugar, preservatives or flavorings and has a reduced sodium content (≈30 mg per 100 ml), making it suitable for people watching their salt intake.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomato juice is rich in lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that gives it a bright red color.
Vegetable juice is often used as a base for soups, sauces and marinades.
Low sodium is achieved by selecting vegetables naturally low in salt and minimizing added salt during production.
Tomato juice is a good alternative to sugary soft drinks because it contains no sugar or artificial sweeteners.
In many markets the product is sold in glass bottles, which helps preserve flavor and aroma.

items.title: Rich in lycopene
items.content: Lycopene helps protect cells from oxidative stress and supports heart health.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains vitamin A and beta‑carotene
items.content: These compounds support vision and skin health.

items.title: Low sodium
items.content: Suitable for low‑salt diets and helps maintain healthy blood pressure.

items.title: Hydration and electrolytes
items.content: The juice provides potassium, important for fluid balance.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes or other vegetables in the blend.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The high acidity can cause heartburn in people sensitive to acidic foods.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Although low, people on strict sodium restriction should account for total daily intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink the juice chilled as a refreshing beverage, add it to smoothies, cocktails, or use it as a base for cold soups (gazpacho) and sauces. A squeeze of lemon or fresh herbs can enhance the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the juice in the refrigerator at 2–6 °C. Once opened, consume within 3–5 days. Do not keep at room temperature for more than 2 hours to prevent microbial growth.
